projects.title: Lunar-regolith rover dust cover
projects.summary: The dust-cover design for a rover’s collection subsystem, with robustness and manufacturability as the goals.
projects.role: Collections sub-team, Cardinal Space Mining; design lead for the dust cover
projects.tools: SolidWorks CAD, ANSYS FEA, Milling, 3D printing

sections.heading: Objective
body: Improve the robustness of the collection subsystem’s dust protection compared with the prior year’s design, while keeping the subsystem functional and manufacturable.

sections.heading: Why it matters
body: > General context: lunar regolith is fine and abrasive, so a mechanism that moves material also has to keep it out of the parts that move.

sections.heading: My contribution
body: I lead the design of the dust cover as part of the Collections sub-team.

sections.heading: Design reasoning
body: The cover cannot be designed on its own. It sits where several requirements meet:
- **Protection and collection motion:** the cover must not impede the parts it protects.
- **Clearance:** gaps small enough to keep material out, large enough to avoid binding.
- **Attachment:** how it mounts to the subsystem.
- **Fabrication:** the team has to be able to build it.

sections.heading: Current stage
body: Design work is ongoing. A final design, prototype, and dust-protection test results do not exist yet.

projects.title: Custom built loft-shelf
projects.summary: A custom-built loft-shelf designed and hand-built for personal use.
projects.tools: SolidWorks CAD, ANSYS FEA, hand fabrication in wood, 3D printing
projects.diagram_label: Illustrative diagram, not the built device

sections.heading: Objective
body: Design, plan, and build a custom loft-shelf for personal use.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
body: The loft-shelf was designed to fit into my lofted bedframe and hold a variety of items. The design needed to be structurally sound, stable (no wobbling or shifting), while also being light-weight and easy to install or relocate if necessary.
Measurments of the bedframe were taken to fit the shelf brackets.
Wood was chosen as the material for the brackets as it is easy to manufacture, while being stiff and sturdy enough to bear the load of the shelf and its contents.

3D-printed PLA was chosen for the shelf itself as it is light-weight, reducing the total load on the brackets and bedframe. The 3D printing process also allowed for a more complex shape that would have been difficult to manufacture with wood.

The shelf was designed with a lip around the top surface to prevent items from sliding off, and sloted rails on the bottom surfaces to fit into the brackets without allowing for slipage or shifting. The shelf was also designed to be easily removable from the brackets if necessary.
An FEA Analysis was used to evaluate the structural integrity of the shelf and brackets, and to ensure that the design would be able to withstand the expected loads.

sections.heading: My contribution
body: This is a Solo Project. I measured the frame the shelf would be fitted to, and designed the shelf in SolidWorks. I also performed finite element analysis (FEA) in ANSYS to ensure the design would be structurally sound, and built the shelf by hand.

projects.title: RL-Trained Robotic Hand
projects.summary: Trained a reinforcement learning model policy to control a robotic hand in Isaac Sim.
projects.tools: Python, Isaac Sim, modern reinforcement learning
projects.diagram_label: Illustrative diagram, not the built device

sections.heading: Objective
body: Train a reinforcement learning model to control a robotic hand. Reference videos and object/hand trajectory data were collected from the HO-Cap (NeurIPS 2025) dataset. The dataset provided data on 21 key points on the robot and human hands, object position and rotation, object linear and angular velocity.
The policy was given the following observations:
- The Robot's hand key points relative to the object
- The Reference hand's key points relative to the object
- The difference between the robot key points and the reference key points
- The next-frame reference points relative to the object
- Current joint positions
- Contact forces acting on each fingertip
Tensorboard was also used to visualize the training process, including the reward function and the policy's performance over time.

sections.heading: Reward function
body: Some information on the reward function used to train the policy:

- During initial training attempts, the agent seemed to have a difficult time learning to grip and pick up the object, even though it seemed to be following the reference path well. For this reason, a strong reward incentive was given for forming a strong, firm, and stable grip on the object.

- Select points on the robots hand determined to be important for a firm grip (all 5 finger tips, palm, and base of the index and middle fingers) are tracked relative to their distance to the object. In the calculation for r_grasp, each of these points are weighted according to their important in forming a strong grip around the object.
- The object's position and rotation are tracked relative to the reference object. The agent is rewarded for keeping the object’s pose as similar to the reference object as possible.

- The amount and speed of movement of the robot’s hand is calculated and penalized. This discourages the agent from making too many unnecessary movements, and encourages a smooth and deliberate trajectory.

sections.heading: My contribution
body: This was a Solo Project. I trained the policy using reinforcement learning, and designed the reward function and action space.

projects.title: Model rocket airbrake system
projects.summary: Proposed airbrake flight-mechanics system for a model rocket.
projects.role: Mechanical sub-team, Cyclone Rocketry; proposed airbrake design

sections.heading: Objective
body: Design an airbrake system that changes a rocket’s drag in flight, as part of designing and developing a model rocket with the Mechanical sub-team.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
body: The airbrakes add drag on demand to help a rocket reach a target apogee.

Previous year's designs, although robust, had a large footprint within the rocket body, and were too heavy. The airbrakes needed to be designed to fit within a smaller profile, while still being able to withstand the forces acting on them during flight.
The spiral cam design would allow for a more compact design without sacrificing control authority
As the fins deployed, the exponentially increasing drag would increase friction on the mechanism, so the design needed to be adjusted to have the fins riding on linear rails
The layout of the motors and how the mechanism fits into the rocket body had to be reconsidered, as the new design was very different from the previous year's.

sections.heading: My contribution
body: I proposed a airbrake concept using a spiral cam, allowing the mechanism to fit into a much smaller profile. I conducted finite element analysis (FEA) simulations in Ansys, and modeled the components in SolidWorks.

projects.title: Substrate rubbing machine
projects.summary: A Substrate rubbing machine designed and built custom for the FMOD Research Lab.
projects.role: Project Manager, led design, construction, and testing

sections.heading: Objective
body: Design, build, test, and deploy a substrate rubbing machine customized for the FMOD Research Lab's needs.

sections.heading: Design Considerations
body: In crystals research, substrate rubbing is used to induce anisotropy or align molecules. Usually this process is done by hand, which can be time consuming and inconsistent.

The FMOD research lab at LUMS needed a machine to automate the process of rubbing substrates. The machine needed to be able to accommodate different substrate sizes, and be able to apply a consistent amount of pressure and speed as a roller was pressed along the substrate. The machine also needed to be easy to operate, and be able to be cleaned and maintained easily.
The control buttons were designed to incorperate as much funtionality as possible, while still being simple to use. The automated rubbing routine would:
- move the roller down to the correct height
- move the substrate bed at a constant velocity under the roller
- when the limit switch at the end of the substrate bed is triggered, the roller is lifted
- the substrate bed is returned to the starting position
The controls also allow for manual positioning of the roller and substrate bed, and isolated control of the roller spin.
These control options were all designed considering the needs of the lab, and the need for a simple and easy to use interface.

sections.heading: My contribution
body: I led the design, construction, and testing of the substrate rubbing machine. With the assistance of the PhysLab team, I outlined the requirements and specifications of the machine, and then designed the machine in Onshape. I also designed a custom PCB for the button panel, 3D printed the control surfaces, and tested the machine before it was deployed to the lab.

projects.title: Private home mediaserver
projects.summary: A Debian server I built and maintain for media, files, photos, and other services I can provide to friends and family.
projects.tools: Debian, Nextcloud, Jellyfin, Immich, Traefik, Pangolin

sections.heading: Objective
body: Run my own file, media, and photo services instead of relying on third-party hosts.

sections.heading: My contribution
body: I built and maintain the server, deploy the services (Nextcloud, Jellyfin, Immich), and troubleshoot problems as they come up.

sections.heading: Technical reasoning
body: Remote access runs through an Oracle VPS using Pangolin and Traefik, a reverse-proxy setup. Making several services reachable behind one entry point means working through routing, proxy integration, and debugging when pieces disagree.
